questions.question: A FastAPI prediction service is fast in a single test but slow under real traffic. The code calls mlflow.sklearn.load_model() inside the /predict function. What is the best fix?
options: Load the model once in the lifespan start-up function and keep it in memory.
Add more fields to the request schema.
Remove the /health endpoint to reduce load.
Switch the response schema from Pydantic to a plain dictionary.
questions.explanation: Loading the model on every request repeats slow disk or registry reads. Loading once at start-up removes that cost. The most tempting wrong option is removing /health, but the health endpoint is cheap and platforms need it; it is not the cause of the slowdown.

questions.question: A client sends alcohol = 40, but the training data only had values from 8 to 15. With Field(ge=8, le=15) in the Pydantic v2 schema, what happens?
options: The model returns a prediction and the value is logged as a warning.
FastAPI returns status 500 because the model fails.
FastAPI returns status 422 with a clear message, and the model is never called.
The value is automatically changed to 15 and a prediction is returned.
questions.explanation: Pydantic rejects the value during validation, so FastAPI returns 422 before the prediction code runs. The most tempting wrong option is the silent prediction with a warning. Without validation, that is what the model would do, which is exactly the problem validation prevents.

questions.question: Which Dockerfile practice is most likely to leak a secret?
options: Using a multi-stage build.
Running the service as a non-root user.
Copying only app.py and the model folder into the image.
Using COPY . . without a .dockerignore file in a folder that contains a .env file.
questions.explanation: COPY . . adds every file in the folder, including a .env file with passwords, and anyone who pulls the image can read it. The most tempting wrong option is the multi-stage build, but it reduces what enters the final image; it does not add secrets.

questions.question: A marketing team needs a churn score for every customer once a month. Which serving approach fits best?
options: Online serving with a p95 latency target of 50 ms.
Batch serving: a scheduled job scores all customers and writes the results to a table.
Shadow deployment of an online API.
Loading the model inside each marketing report.
questions.explanation: The inputs are known in advance and nobody waits for a single answer, so a scheduled batch job is simpler and cheaper. The most tempting wrong option is online serving. It would work, but it adds an always-on service and latency targets that this use case does not need.

questions.question: A team wants to compare a new triage model with the current one on real cases, without the new model affecting any patient. Which release strategy fits?
options: Canary release to 5% of patients.
Blue-green switch of all traffic at once.
Shadow deployment: the new model scores copies of real requests, but only the old model's output is shown.
Deleting the old model so that only the new one runs.
questions.explanation: Shadow deployment tests on real traffic while users only see the current model, so there is no risk to patients. The most tempting wrong option is a canary. A canary still shows the new model's output to some real users, which the team wants to avoid.
